overview.title: 📖 Overview: Borders, Bridges, and a New Exemption
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 55a–55b
overview.hebrewSource: רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹמֵר: הַיַּרְדֵּן מַפְסִיק לְמַעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf resolves the debate over how many animals bridge distant flocks by reinterpreting a challenging baraita, then raises Rav Pappa's extension of Shmuel's view to even a shepherd's tools or dog. It then turns to Rabbi Meir's ruling that the Jordan River itself divides flocks for tithing purposes regardless of distance, and Rabbi Ami's qualification that a bridge reunites them. A close look at the biblical text asks whether the Jordan is truly a border, or even part of the Land of Israel at all, launching a broader excursus on the world's rivers — their sources, names, and halakhic uses — before the daf closes with a fresh mishna: one who purchases an animal, or receives one as a gift, is exempt from separating animal tithe on it.

slides.title: 🐕 Sharpening Shmuel's Rule
slides.subtitle: How little does it take to bridge two distant flocks?

lines.speaker: Baraita
lines.text: Five sheep in Kfar Ḥananya and five in Kfar Otnai (32 mil apart) don't combine unless there's also one sheep in Tzippori, between them — a challenge to Rav's 'five in the middle' rule.

lines.speaker: Shmuel resolves
lines.text: Not really five and five — the case is nine and nine, with just one in the middle bridging both nines to reach ten on either side. This fits Rav too.

lines.speaker: Rav Pappa extends
lines.text: For Shmuel, even just the SHEPHERD himself in the middle — without any sheep — bridges the two flocks. Even his tools left there would suffice, since he must go collect them.

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi's open question
lines.text: What about the shepherd's dog in the middle? Since it usually comes when called, maybe it doesn't count — but sometimes he must go fetch it himself. Unresolved (teiku).

slides.title: 🌊 The Jordan River Divides — Unless Bridged
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir's ruling and its exact textual basis

nodes.content: 📜 Rabbi Meir: the Jordan River separates flocks for animal tithe, regardless of distance
🌉 Rabbi Ami: only true when there's no bridge — a bridge reunites the two banks
❓ Objection: a baraita says flocks on opposite riverbanks, or even in two adjoining provinces with NO water between them, still don't combine — so it's not just about physical proximity!

✅ Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba (citing R' Yoḥanan): the real reason is textual — 'the Jordan shall be its border' (Joshua 18:20) makes the river a border in its own right, a formal legal boundary, not merely a physical obstacle

slides.title: 🗺️ Is the Jordan Part of the Land of Israel?
slides.subtitle: A dispute among tanna'im with real consequences for the border ruling
rows: The Jordan is NOT part of the land of Canaan
'When you pass over the Jordan INTO the land' — implies the Jordan itself is not that land
The Jordan IS part of the land of Canaan
Just as Jericho (across the Jordan) is called Canaan, so is the river itself
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba's view fits Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira (Jordan = a border unto itself)
Rabbi Ami's original 'no bridge' reasoning would need all rivers to count, which the mishna doesn't say

slides.title: 💧 A River Digression: Names, Sources, and Uses
slides.subtitle: Rabbinic geography before returning to halakha

boxes.title: The Jordan's Course
items: Emerges from the Cave of Pamyas
Flows through Lake Ḥula, the Sea of Galilee, and the Dead Sea
Called 'Jordan' (yored, 'descends') specifically from Beit Jericho southward

boxes.title: The Euphrates
items: Rav: source of the other three rivers of Eden
Named 'Perat' because its waters are 'fruitful and multiply' (parim)
Halakhic use: one who vows against 'water from the Euphrates' broadly is barred from ALL water everywhere

callout.label: Practical impact:
callout.text: Shmuel's father made his daughters a standing mikveh in Nisan (rainy season, concerned about flowing rainwater) but let them immerse directly in the Euphrates in Tishrei, when the water was purely from the river's own source.

slides.title: 🎁 New Mishna: Purchased and Gifted Animals Are Exempt
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: One who purchases an animal, or receives one as a gift, is exempt from separating animal tithe on it. This sets up the next daf's inquiry into the verse's source for this exemption — comparing it to the redemption of a firstborn son, which likewise applies only to one's own biological child, never a purchased or adopted one.
slides.hebrewSource: הַלּוֹקֵחַ, אוֹ שֶׁנִּיתַּן לוֹ בְּמַתָּנָה — פָּטוּר מִמַּעְשַׂר בְּהֵמָה

summary.principle: Animal tithe requires genuine physical and legal proximity within one owner's flock — the Jordan River creates a formal halakhic border regardless of distance, while a bridge, or even a shepherd's mere presence, can reunite what would otherwise be separated.

flowSteps.content: 🐕 Rav Pappa: for Shmuel, even the shepherd alone (or his tools) in the middle bridges two flocks
🌊 Rabbi Meir: the Jordan River divides flocks for tithing, regardless of distance — a formal border, not just an obstacle

columns.content: 🌉 A bridge reunites the two banks (R' Ami)
💧 Digression on world rivers, their names and halakhic vow implications

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: a purchased or gifted animal is exempt from animal tithe entirely — the mitzva applies only to animals born into one's own herd

quiz.q: How does Shmuel's opinion explain the baraita where five sheep in one village and five in another (32 mil apart) require an additional sheep in the middle village to combine?
o: It refutes Shmuel entirely
The baraita really means nine and nine sheep, with one in the middle bridging each group to ten
It only applies to goats, not sheep
The baraita is not about animal tithe at all
quiz.e: Shmuel reinterprets the baraita as involving nine sheep on each side, so the single sheep in the middle can combine with either group of nine to reach the required ten — consistent with his 'even one' rule.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, why does the Jordan River specifically (rather than any water barrier) divide flocks for animal tithe?
o: Because it is simply too wide to cross
Because a verse (Joshua 18:20) renders the Jordan a formal border in its own right, not because of mere physical difficulty
Because fish live in it
Because it is the only river mentioned in the Torah
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir's ruling rests on the Jordan being explicitly called a border in Joshua 18:20, making it a formal halakhic boundary — distinguishing it from Rabbi Ami's earlier physical-obstacle reasoning, which would apply to any uncrossable river.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Ami, what happens to Rabbi Meir's rule that the Jordan divides flocks if there is a bridge across the river?
o: The rule still applies fully
The bridge reunites the two banks, so the flocks combine
Bridges are irrelevant to this halakha
A bridge makes the separation even stronger
quiz.e: Rabbi Ami teaches that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies only where there is no bridge; where a bridge exists, it functionally reunites the two sides, allowing the flocks to combine for tithing.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's view (cited in the dispute about whether the Jordan is part of the land of Canaan), what is the implication of the phrase 'when you pass over the Jordan into the land'?
o: The Jordan River itself is part of the land of Canaan
The Jordan River is NOT part of the land of Canaan, since one 'passes over' it to reach the land
The verse has no bearing on the Jordan's status
The Jordan is holier than the land itself
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira reads 'into the land' as indicating that crossing the Jordan gets you INTO the land of Canaan, implying the river itself stands outside that category.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna at the end of the daf, is a person obligated to separate animal tithe from an animal they purchased or received as a gift?
o: Yes, exactly as with animals born into their own herd
No — such a person is exempt from animal tithe on that animal
Only if it was a gift, not a purchase
Only outside Eretz Yisrael
quiz.e: The mishna states plainly that one who purchases an animal or receives one as a gift is exempt from separating animal tithe on it — the obligation applies only to animals born into one's own flock.
